title: Psychoanalysis and School Psychology: Toward a Psychoanalytically Informed Framework for Educational Practice
abstract: ABSTRACT Although the relationship between psychoanalysis and education has long been marked by tension—not least because the two fields approach the human subject from different epistemological and institutional positions—both have much to offer to each other by deepening understanding of students, learning, and educational life. Moreover, contemporary school psychology has developed into a prevention‐oriented, systems‐based profession with strong commitments to assessment, intervention, consultation, and evidence‐based practice. Yet this development has also left comparatively less room for sustained attention to unconscious communication, defensive processes, emotional meaning, and the affective life of educational institutions. This paper argues that psychoanalytic thinking offers school psychology a distinctive reflective framework for understanding educational difficulties as unconscious, relational, and institutional phenomena. Drawing on key psychoanalytic and group‐analytic traditions, the paper examines how concepts such as transference, countertransference, containment, holding, symbolization, and social defense can deepen understanding of classroom life, teacher–student relationships, school culture, and family–school work. It further proposes that a psychoanalytically informed school psychologist does not function as a clinician within the school, but as a reflective practitioner who can collaborate with school communities in thinking more deeply about behavior, anxiety, conflict, exclusion, and the emotional meanings attached to learning. The paper also considers the limits and risks of this perspective, including time pressures, accountability demands, institutional resistance, and the danger of overinterpretation. It concludes that psychoanalysis does not replace school psychology; rather, it expands its interpretive and ethical capacities by restoring attention to the emotional and unconscious dimensions of educational practice.
